Izinyoka - Illegal Connections

By: Chwayitisa Futshane | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
hundreds of South African households are illegally connecting to the grid with dangerous consequences.

Summary:
With government unable to provide electricity to hundreds of households throughout South Africa, people are turning to Izinyoka, to provide electricity to households in the informal settlements.

Izinyoka is the colloquil name given to young men who use wires to connect illegally to the grid, but this is a dangerous undertaking, not only yo the Izoinyoka, but to young children caught in the cross fire of exposed high voltage wiring.

And Eskom battles to keep the lights on in ordinary suburbs, it seems that there is very little it can do to stop this growing trend.

Trevor Ngwane is a UJ doctorate student and social activist who has been helping Izinyoka for years to connect to the grid.

We also speak to two mothers from the EC who lost their children after they were electrocuted by live wires while playing outside.


Further information:
And Eskom battles to keep the lights on in ordinary suburbs, it seems that there is very little it can do to stop this growing trend.

Electricity theft, has also spread across the Eastern Cape province with two metros reporting losses of hundreds of millions of rands every year.
Buffalo City Metro (BCM) lost an average of R88-million a year while Nelson Mandela Bay Metro (NMBM) reports losses of R100-million.
In three years 28 BCM residents, many of them children, have died because of izinyoka.
Two of the victims are 9-year-old Thembelihle Rubushe of Duncan Village and a 10-year-old Sihle Mva of Amalinda. Both were electrocuted when they stepped on exposed illegal wire connections.

Izinyoka includes meter tampering and non-registered meters, said BCM spokesman Thandy Matebese.
He said BCM had recorded “non-technical” losses of R88-million.
NMBM Mthubanzi Mniki said they had launched preventative programmes. The metro is running awareness campaigns in communities.
“We also electrify shacks and use alternative non-grid electrification like solar energy. We cut down all illegal connections,” he said.
“We are losing over R100-million a year on this.”
BCM mayor Alfred Mtsi has appealed to BCM communities to put a stop to illegal connections.
“These persistent acts of illegal connections incur unnecessary costs to the municipality and expose people to fatal dangers,” said Mtsi.
Mtsi said disadvantaged BCM communities had benefited from the electrification of an additional 1000 informal dwellings in Mdantsane and Duncan Village.
BCM East Bank resident, Neville Varrie complained their area did not have street lights.
They asked BCM to act “but all these officials are telling us is that the reason for this is that we are stealing electricity and that’s a lie. We don’t do that here. We suffer now because of other people’s izinyoka,” said Varrie.



Trevor Ngwane is a UJ doctorate student and social activist who has been helping Izinyoka for years to connect to the grid.

We can speak to an illegal connector who will speak to us about why he risks his life and those of others to do this and the BCM in East London.

We also speak to two mothers from the EC who lost their children after they were electrocuted by live wires while playing outside.

One day shoot in East London to film two mothers who's young children were electrocuted recently in the Eastern Cape.

Press Release:


Stealing Power
They call themselves the Izinyoka. And, these illegal electricity connectors will stop at almost nothing to provide free electricity to informal settlement homes. They risk life and limb to break into high voltage transformers, city street lights – any source of electricity – to install live electrical leads that often stretch across fields and roads for kilometres. Carte Blanche reveals the shocking extent to which Izinyoka have tapped into the country’s already unstable power supply.


Script:


Script
VO: A fire blazes through the dry winter grass. Choking thick smoke fills the air as the flames get dangerously close to Princess Informal Settlement in Roodepoort.

VO: But this fire wasn’t caused by a cigarette carelessly tossed from a car window.
It’s the work of Izinyoka – informally trained men who use live uncovered wires, haphazardly pulled together, to draw electricity from any possible power source, to illegally supply nearby informal settlements.

UPSOUND[03:46:42] Trevor: … Izinyoka was a negative campaign by Eskom whereby people who connect themselves are called snakes...

VO: Trevor Ngwane is a well known social activist in Soweto and one of the leaders of the Soweto Electricity Crisis Committee or SECC, an organization which was formed to fight for the right to free electricity.

UPSOUND Trevor [03:47:14] ... when you’ve got Izinyoka, it means you’ve got electricity. … So it’s ok now. You can call it Izinyoka.

LINK: It all started about 16 years ago when Eskom introduced a ‘user must pay’ policy for electricity throughout the country, so thousands of people who used to pay a flat rate of about R24 a month, just couldn’t afford the new tariffs.

UPSOUND [03:27:59] Trevor: In those days, electricity was cheap.

That flat rate had been made even cheaper in order to get people to stop boycotting payments.

Then suddenly there was payment by consumption, which means you paid according to how much you consumed. That made rises of up to?? 200%, 300% in terms of the amount you paid.




VO: So Eskom started disconnecting all non paying customers.

UPSOUND [03:29:11] Trevor: There was a lot of anger, there was a lot of suffering... So it was quite bad for Soweto. In fact Soweto … according to Eskom, they were cutting off at a rate of 20 000 houses per month, so itwas going to become a dark city.

UPSOUND [03:30:05] Trevor: … So that pushed us into what we called Operation Khanyisa
UPSOUND [03:31:31] Trevor: …. We trained, you know, youngsters to reconnect the electricity, we did it for free and we made people feel that …they had a right to it.

LINK: For many years, he’s been teaching izinyoka to connect to the grid and, despite the apparent danger, Trevor insists that electricity is a basic human right.

UPSOUND [03:30:49] Trevor: … I think every human being in modern times has a right to electricity. You know, kids doing matric, studying with a candle. Old dears, old grannies with fading eyes – they need electricity.

VO: Thembelihle informal settlement is one area where members of the SECC have trained illegal connectors.

There we met Bhayisa Miya, an unemployed father of two. He’s been illegally connecting his informal settlement for the past five years.

UPSOUND TCR: 04:19:13:20 Bhayisa:
‘cause you remember there was a World Cup in 2010… I remember it was in February. Because we wanted to (be) part of the excited of the World Cup, we connected ourselves.

LINK: Now in this case it starts with the transformer. The door just happens to be unlocked, despite all the warnings. Inside you find the connections. The yellow ones belong to City Power. The red, white and blue are the work of illegal connectors.
VO: Bhayisa is part of a group of organized illegal connectors who connected 47 homes from the informal settlement to this transformer.

TCR: 04:21:48:15 Derek: Bhayisa, this has to go a long way to the houses across the road, can you show us how the electricity gets there?

Bhayisa: Ya, you are welcome, I can show you.

VO: Many of the cables used are old and have been supplying electricity to the community for years, leaving them in the worst possible condition.

UPSOUND TCR: 04:22:27:04 Derek: Bhayisa, a lot of these cables are exposed.
Bhayisa: Ya they are exposed.
Derek: So you’re saying if I touch this, I will get fried?
Bhayisa: You will. I think most definitely you will.

VO: He showed us how their cables are pulled from the transformer, over the electricity poles or underground through the storm water drain, all the way to Thembelihle.

VO: At home Bhayisa runs a small business selling cooldrinks, so he needs electricity for his fridge, to keep his products cold.

He also uses power for the lights, a small stove and his television set.

UPSOUND TCR: 04:39:37:12 Derek:
Do you think it’s fair what you’re doing? Some people say it’s theft.

Bhayisa:
I’ve heard people complaining of one day of load shedding, one day, of a few hours, so what about us, without electricity for years and years. I’ve been here in Thembelihle, for more than 25 years, without electricity.
UPSOUND [03:25:57] Trevor:...some informal settlements, they do it in an organised fashion. Such as Thembelihle. So they come together, they try and keep it safe. But others… there’s more chaos.


VO: That’s when Izinyoka use uninsulated wires to connect to the grid.

VO: We went to Protea South Community Clinic, which is situated in another informal settlement, where Izinyoka are causing constant power outages at the treatment centre.

UPSOUND TCR: 05:01:37:12 Nonceba:
It has very negatively affected the clinic, because … We have immunization vaccines that we cannot immunize children if the vaccine has not been kept in a proper cold chain ….

VO: Nonceba Molwele is a Member of the Mayoral Committee for Health and Social Development in the City of Johannesburg and she spoke on behalf of the clinic.

She says that the healthcare centre now relies permanently on this generator.

UPSOUND Nonceba: In a severe situation, we take our vaccines, we put them in a cooler box, we get ice, … and we transport our vaccines to the nearest clinic.

VO: But for the clinic, it doesn’t end there. Despite having security on the premises, even the generator has become an easy source of power for izinyoka.
UPSOUND Nonceba TCR 05:08:00:23
They have already intimidated security because they want access to the generator. We have fenced the generator but as they cut the fence, they have already started fiddling with the generator.

VO: City Power has been battling illegal connections for years and according to Stuart Webb, the director of engineering operations, it’s a losing battle.
UPSOUND Stuart Webb TCR: 14:05:44:10
We regularly go into areas and sweep them clean of the illegal connections, but unfortunately we are finding that within a day or two they are all returned and installed again.

VO: And it’s not just an issue for City Power, but for the National Power supplier, Eskom.

UPSOUND 16:30 Maboe

Its seriously dangerous when you look at what can happen - one mistake, that person can be electrocuted and die or be severely injured,

They are also putting the community they are operating in danger.

UPSOUND [03:38:06] Trevor: It’s dangerous for the children. But now the people, they weigh, you know, the danger against the benefit.
UPSOUND TCR: 05:04:53:03 Nonceba:
There is no justification to illegally connect. There is no justification to steal power from the clinic.




VO: In most cases, the illegal connections are done using bare non-insulated wires, which run along the ground or over trees and anybody coming into contact with these live wires could be electrocuted.

LINK: Here in Roodepoort it’s spaghetti junction - a tangle of exposed wires coming out of the transformer, some of them going out under the road, others just strung over this lamp post… all of them heading to the Princess informal settlement.

LINK: On the other side of the road, there’s a string of totally bare cables, no insulation whatsoever.

VO: These wires run across an open veldt, all the way to Princess informal settlement.
LINK: It’s really like a war zone, but instead of landmines, you’ve got these lethal cables. It’s beyond belief, I can tell you.

VO: In the past year, Eskom recorded 18 fatalities relating to illegal connections, but they say many injuries and deaths go unreported.

VO: But aside from the obvious risk of electrocution for individuals, these bare live pieces of wire, could pose an even bigger hazard to entire communities.

LINK: And this is just one of the results of all of these exposed wires; they obviously touch at some stage, a few sparks and a fire runs out of control. Look how close it is to the informal settlement.


VO: But there’s also a massive financial impact on City Power, as they continue to count the cost of illegal connections.
UPSOUND Stuart Webb: We have figures which indicate that we are losing a certain percentage of our revenue because of illegal connections. Last year the recorded figure was around 19%.



VO: This means City Power lost an estimated R3 billion in the last financial year. Almost a fifth of its total income.






VO: From Princess Informal Settlement we headed for Lenasia.

Here, on Mecca Road, most of the transformers belong to Eskom and Izinyoka make no effort to hide the uncovered live wires.


VO: Eskom believes that there are no easy solutions to putting an end to illegal connections and they insist that supplying electricity to informal settlements isn’t an option.


UPSOUND TCR 04:46 ESKOM Maboe
It’s simple people who need the service. They are not getting the service because … you are not allowed as a utility to give that type of service to people in areas that are not proclaimed for settlement.

VO: City Power has however decided to take the drastic step of providing electricity to informal settlements. A process that could take up to five years to complete.
UPSOUND Stuart Webb TCR: 14:07:30:23
…I’m quite confident that when we start to roll out electricity towards all these areas, the level of illegal connections will drastically come down.

VO: In the meantime, illegally connecting to the grid is still an easy alternative for poor communities.









PROMOS
15 Seconds
1.) Izinyoka or illegal connectors will use almost any method to source electricity... with deadly consequences.
UPSOUND: Bhayisa Miya “There are people who have been electrocuted to death by these same illegal connections.”

2.) They believe free electricity is a basic human right. But who’s training hundreds of young men to connect illegally to the grid?
UPSOUND: Trevor Ngwane “We trained youngsters to reconnect the electricity, we did it for free.”
10 Second\In studio
1.) As the national power supplier continues to take strain, illegal connectors will stop at nothing to provide electricity to some of the country’s poorest.

UPSOUND 16:30 Maboe Its seriously dangerous when you look at what can happen - one mistake, that person can be electrocuted and die or be severely injured, They are also putting the community they are operating in danger. UPSOUND [03:38:06] Trevor: It’s dangerous for the children. But now the people, they weigh, you know, the danger against the benefit. UPSOUND TCR: 05:04:53:03 Nonceba: There is no justification to illegally connect. There is no justification to steal power from the clinic. VO: In most cases, the illegal connections are done using bare non-insulated wires, which run along the ground or over trees and anybody coming into contact with these live wires could be electrocuted. LINK: Here in Roodepoort it’s spaghetti junction - a tangle of exposed wires coming out of the transformer, some of them going out under the road, others just strung over this lamp post… all of them heading to the Princess informal settlement. LINK: On the other side of the road, there’s a string of totally bare cables, no insulation whatsoever. VO: These wires run across an open veldt, all the way to Princess informal settlement. LINK: It’s really like a war zone, but instead of landmines, you’ve got these lethal cables. It’s beyond belief, I can tell you. VO: In the past year, Eskom recorded 18 fatalities relating to illegal connections, but they say many injuries and deaths go unreported. VO: But aside from the obvious risk of electrocution for individuals, these bare live pieces of wire, could pose an even bigger hazard to entire communities. LINK: And this is just one of the results of all of these exposed wires; they obviously touch at some stage, a few sparks and a fire runs out of control. Look how close it is to the informal settlement. VO: But there’s also a massive financial impact on City Power, as they continue to count the cost of illegal connections. UPSOUND Stuart Webb: We have figures which indicate that we are losing a certain percentage of our revenue because of illegal connections. Last year the recorded figure was around 19%. VO: This means City Power lost an estimated R3 billion in the last financial year. Almost a fifth of its total income. VO: From Princess Informal Settlement we headed for Lenasia. Here, on Mecca Road, most of the transformers belong to Eskom and Izinyoka make no effort to hide the uncovered live wires. VO: Eskom believes that there are no easy solutions to putting an end to illegal connections and they insist that supplying electricity to informal settlements isn’t an option. UPSOUND TCR 04:46 ESKOM Maboe It’s simple people who need the service. They are not getting the service because … you are not allowed as a utility to give that type of service to people in areas that are not proclaimed for settlement. VO: City Power has however decided to take the drastic step of providing electricity to informal settlements. A process that could take up to five years to complete. UPSOUND Stuart Webb TCR: 14:07:30:23 …I’m quite confident that when we start to roll out electricity towards all these areas, the level of illegal connections will drastically come down. VO: In the meantime, illegally connecting to the grid is still an easy alternative for poor communities. PROMOS 15 Seconds 1.) Izinyoka or illegal connectors will use almost any method to source electricity... with deadly consequences. UPSOUND: Bhayisa Miya “There are people who have been electrocuted to death by these same illegal connections.” 2.) They believe free electricity is a basic human right. But who’s training hundreds of young men to connect illegally to the grid? UPSOUND: Trevor Ngwane “We trained youngsters to reconnect the electricity, we did it for free.” 10 Second\In studio 1.) As the national power supplier continues to take strain, illegal connectors will stop at nothing to provide electricity to some of the country’s poorest.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): hundreds of South African households are illegally connecting to the grid with dangerous consequences.
metadata.Summary: With government unable to provide electricity to hundreds of households throughout South Africa, people are turning to Izinyoka, to provide electricity to households in the informal settlements. Izinyoka is the colloquil name given to young men who use wires to connect illegally to the grid, but this is a dangerous undertaking, not only yo the Izoinyoka, but to young children caught in the cross fire of exposed high voltage wiring. And Eskom battles to keep the lights on in ordinary suburbs, it seems that there is very little it can do to stop this growing trend. Trevor Ngwane is a UJ doctorate student and social activist who has been helping Izinyoka for years to connect to the grid. We also speak to two mothers from the EC who lost their children after they were electrocuted by live wires while playing outside.
metadata.Further information: And Eskom battles to keep the lights on in ordinary suburbs, it seems that there is very little it can do to stop this growing trend. Electricity theft, has also spread across the Eastern Cape province with two metros reporting losses of hundreds of millions of rands every year. Buffalo City Metro (BCM) lost an average of R88-million a year while Nelson Mandela Bay Metro (NMBM) reports losses of R100-million. In three years 28 BCM residents, many of them children, have died because of izinyoka. Two of the victims are 9-year-old Thembelihle Rubushe of Duncan Village and a 10-year-old Sihle Mva of Amalinda. Both were electrocuted when they stepped on exposed illegal wire connections. Izinyoka includes meter tampering and non-registered meters, said BCM spokesman Thandy Matebese. He said BCM had recorded “non-technical” losses of R88-million. NMBM Mthubanzi Mniki said they had launched preventative programmes. The metro is running awareness campaigns in communities. “We also electrify shacks and use alternative non-grid electrification like solar energy. We cut down all illegal connections,” he said. “We are losing over R100-million a year on this.” BCM mayor Alfred Mtsi has appealed to BCM communities to put a stop to illegal connections. “These persistent acts of illegal connections incur unnecessary costs to the municipality and expose people to fatal dangers,” said Mtsi. Mtsi said disadvantaged BCM communities had benefited from the electrification of an additional 1000 informal dwellings in Mdantsane and Duncan Village. BCM East Bank resident, Neville Varrie complained their area did not have street lights. They asked BCM to act “but all these officials are telling us is that the reason for this is that we are stealing electricity and that’s a lie. We don’t do that here. We suffer now because of other people’s izinyoka,” said Varrie. Trevor Ngwane is a UJ doctorate student and social activist who has been helping Izinyoka for years to connect to the grid. We can speak to an illegal connector who will speak to us about why he risks his life and those of others to do this and the BCM in East London. We also speak to two mothers from the EC who lost their children after they were electrocuted by live wires while playing outside.
